'''Betty Lou Raskin''' (April 9, 1924<ref>Dates of birth and death for Betty L. Raskin per the United States Social Security Death Index</ref> – December 17, 2010) was an American chemist who researched plastics in the 1950s and 1960s. A [[Maryland]]er, she grew up in [[Baltimore]] and obtained a chemistry degree to begin work at the radiation laboratory of [[Johns Hopkins University]].

One of the primary products she developed while researching [[polystyrene]] was a foamed version that she turned into an opaque smoke good for military signaling, [[skywriting]], and potential contamination protection. A part of multiple scientific organizations, she used her membership to promote women in science and spoke out against the cultural discrimination of intelligent and successful women.

==Childhood and education==
Born in 1924<ref name="thesis">{{Cite thesis |last=Raskin |first=Betty Lou |title=The Relative Effect of Occupational and Socio-occupational Information on High School Girls' Expressed Opinions of Women Scientists and Science as a Career |date=1968 |degree=Ph.D. |publisher=Johns Hopkins University |oclc=30731041}}</ref> to a [[face doctor]] father Moses Raskin and a [[Nursing management|superintendent]] of [[nursing]] mother Rose Frank Raskin, Raskin was raised in Baltimore and attended the Robert E. Lee Accelerate Junior High School. She went on to graduate from [[Western High School (Maryland)|Western High School]] in 1940 and attended [[Goucher College]] to earn a [[Bachelor's degree]] in chemistry. Continuing her education at Johns Hopkins University, she went on to earn a [[Master's degree]] in chemistry and a [[Ph.D.]] in [[educational psychology]].<ref name="Sun">{{cite news |last=Jacques |first=Kelly |date=December 31, 2010 |title=Betty Lou Raskin, Hopkins researcher, dies |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2010/12/31/betty-lou-raskin-hopkins-researcher-dies/|url-access=subscription|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240114193417/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2010/12/31/betty-lou-raskin-hopkins-researcher-dies/|archive-date=January 14, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |access-date=January 14, 2024}}</ref> Her 1968 dissertation was titled ''The Relative Effect of Occupational and Socio-occupational Information on High School Girls' Expressed Opinions of Women Scientists and Science as a Career''.<ref name="thesis" />

==Career==
After graduation, Raskin spent several years at the [[Homewood Campus]] in charge of the radiation laboratory's research branch on plastics. According to Raskin, she was the only woman researching polystyrene in the United States during the 1950s. By 1967, the US government stopped providing [[Grant (money)|research grants]] for plastics research,<ref name="Sun"/> leading Raskin to leave her position at the Johns Hopkins lab and becoming a psychology lecturer and assistant professor at [[Towson University]] while she worked on obtaining her Ph.D.<ref name="Jones">{{cite news |last=Jones |first=Stacy V. |date=February 17, 1968 |title='Holey Smoke,' Says Air Force Of Lady Chemist's Invention |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-tribune-holey-smoke-says-ai/139066768/ |work=[[The Scranton Times-Tribune]] |access-date=January 20, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> She also changed her research focus to [[consumer behavior]], a new area of study at the time, that she taught as [[interdisciplinary]] between psychology and business.<ref name="Sun"/>

Frequently speaking out about the ability of women in science, Raskin was a long-term advocate for the advancement and inclusion of women scientists. During the late 1950s, she noted that she was one of around 500 women in the [[American Chemical Society]] out of over ten thousand members. She stated that it was the incorrect idea of women scientists being "abnormal, unfeminine" that prevented women from deciding to enter scientific fields of study.<ref name="Shuman">{{cite news |last=Shuman |first=Nicholas |date=September 11, 1958 |title=Female Chemist Sees Scientist – Need Answer |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/fort-worth-star-telegram-female-chemist/138913664/ |work=[[Fort Worth Star-Telegram]] |access-date=January 16, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> She presented a paper to the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] in December 1958 on how the "brainpower" of women is being wasted by society and general media by not portraying the capabilities of women in science,<ref name="Sun2"/> with her talk at the meeting being titled "American Women: Unclaimed Treasures of Science".<ref>{{cite news |last=Poole |first=Lynn |date=May 9, 1959 |title=Women Have Brains, Says Scientist, and Her Work Proves It |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-buffalo-news-women-have-brains-says/139059810/ |work=[[The Buffalo News]] |access-date=January 18, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> In her presentation, she blamed the media for making the [[mink coat]] the "symbol of female success" and not the [[lab coat]].<ref name="Sun2"/> An article she wrote on April 19, 1959, in the ''[[New York Times]]'' titled "Woman's Place Is in the Lab, Too",<ref>{{cite news |last=Raskin |first=Betty Lou |date=April 19, 1959 |title=Woman's Place Is in the Lab, Too |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1959/04/19/archives/womans-place-is-in-the-lab-too-how-can-we-fill-our-need-for-more.html |work=[[New York Times]] |access-date=January 20, 2024}}</ref> where she discussed issues facing women in science and societal pressures against women joining scientific fields, was highly commented upon in the media and by the rest of the scientific community.<ref>{{cite book |last=Puaca |first=Laura Micheletti |date=2014 |title=Searching for Scientific Womanpower: Technocratic Feminism and the Politics of National Security, 1940–1980 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=84RgAwAAQBAJ |publisher=[[University of North Carolina Press]] |pages=91–95 |isbn=9781469610818}}</ref>

===Patents===
Raskin's work in plastics research resulted in several new methodologies and techniques developed by her for specialized production. A grant from the [[US Air Force]]'s [[Wright Air Development Command]] had her create a method for "fluffing" plastic particles in the air, which she patented as "Holey Smoke" in 1960,<ref>{{cite news |last=Blakeslee |first=Alton |date=April 8, 1959 |title=Rings in orbit? 'Holey' plastic smoke'll make them |newspaper=The Peninsula Times Tribune |page=3 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-peninsula-times-tribune-rings-in-orb/139058199/ |agency=[[Associated Press]] |access-date=January 18, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> though originally referred to as "flokes".<ref>{{cite news |last=Miller |first=James N. |date=July 20, 1961 |title=Betty Lou Raskin Knows Her Smokes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/lancaster-eagle-gazette-betty-lou-raskin/139215342/ |work=[[Lancaster Eagle-Gazette]] |access-date=January 20, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> The commercial patent was later bought by [[Dow Chemical]] and had usability in [[skywriting]], [[Smoke screen|smokescreens]], [[cloud seeding]], and protecting farmland from frost.<ref>{{cite magazine |author=<!--not stated--> |date=January 27, 1961 |title=Science: Holey Smoke |url=https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,826804,00.html |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |access-date=January 16, 2024}}</ref> The US government kept a free license to use the material and the Air Force aimed to use it for signaling purposes, because of its capability to give dimensionality to lights and images projected on it.<ref name="Jones"/> Raskin also suggested in her 1959 American Chemical Society presentation that since the smoke is able to provide a shield against contamination, including in the air, that it could be used to shield against the effects of nuclear explosions.<ref>{{cite news |last=Fenton |first=John H. |date=April 9, 1959 |title=Smoke Proposed As Atomic Shield |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/114914385 |work=[[New York Times]] |access-date=January 20, 2024 |id={{ProQuest|114914385}} }}</ref>

==Research==
During her time as a research associate at the Homewood radiation laboratory, Raskin focused on foamed plastics (polystyrene). She described in a presentation to the [[American Chemical Society]] that the new expanded foams could be used for construction of a house and provide [[Thermal insulation|insulation]] at the same time.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=September 14, 1955 |title=Home Of Air And Plastic Possible |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-news-messenger-home-of-air-and-plast/138908659/ |work=[[The News-Messenger]] |access-date=January 16, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

==Organizations==
Raskin was a member of the [[Society of Plastics Engineers]]<ref name="Sun"/> and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS).<ref name="Sun2">{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=December 30, 1958 |title=Woman Scientist Says U.S. Wastes Female Brainpower |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-baltimore-sun-woman-scientist-says-u/139053802/ |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |pages=26, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-baltimore-sun-woman-scientist-says-u/139055042/ 17] |access-date=January 18, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> She became a member of the American Chemical Society in 1948 and later the Maryland representative to the national conference.<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--not stated--> |date=March 31, 1964 |title=Miss Raskin To Attend Chemical Unit Meeting |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-baltimore-sun-miss-raskin-to-attend/139066276/ |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |access-date=January 20, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>
